notes.short: Milk for infants: the first and simplest teaching
notes.about: Paul says he could not speak to the Corinthians as spiritual, but as infants in Christ. He calls the first, simplest teaching milk, and the deeper truths solid food, which they were not ready for. And they are still not ready, though by now they should have grown up.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: I gave you milk, not solid food
figure.means: milk is the simplest first truths of the gospel, fit for those still infants in Christ; solid food is the deeper truths, for those grown in faith

notes.evidence: Barnes says Paul continues the metaphor drawn from feeding infants: milk is the simple first doctrines, meat the deeper ones, as in Hebrews 5. T. Teignmouth Shore (Ellicott) says the word infant suggests the two images of milk and meat, for the simpler truths and the higher wisdom. Benson says milk alludes to the proper food of babes, and meat means the higher truths.

cites.quote: Paul here continues the metaphor, which is derived from the custom of feeding infants with the lightest food. Milk here evidently denotes the more simple and elementary doctrines of Christianity - the doctrines of the new birth, of repentance, faith, etc. The same figure occurs in Heb 5:11-14 ... "Meat" here denotes the more sublime and mysterious doctrines of religion.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The use of the word “infant” naturally suggests these two images for the higher wisdom and for the simpler truths of the gospel respectively. ... He does not blame them for having been “babes” at the outset, but he does in the following passage blame them for not having yet grown up out of infancy.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: even mere babes in Christ; as little acquainted with, and experienced in, the things of God, as babes are with respect to the things of the world. ... alluding to milk being the proper food of babes: not with meat The higher truths of Christianity; such as are more difficult to be understood, received, and practised
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Paul planted, Apollos watered, God made it grow
notes.about: Paul carries a farming picture through four verses: he planted the seed, Apollos watered it, but God made it grow. The picture shows that the workers serve together in God's field, and that the growth comes from God alone.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: I planted the seed and Apollos watered it
figure.means: Paul's first preaching, which founded the church at Corinth, and Apollos's later teaching, both made fruitful by God alone

notes.evidence: John Calvin says Paul shows the nature of the ministry by a similitude: the word is seed and ministers are like husbandmen. Albert Barnes says Paul compares founding the church to planting, a figure from farming. T. Teignmouth Shore (Ellicott) calls it an image borrowed from farming; Simon Browne (Henry's commentary) calls it a metaphor: they only plant and water; God's blessing gives the fruit.
notes.limit: In verse 9 the picture of a field gives way to a building, which verses 10 to 15 carry on.

cites.quote: He unfolds more clearly the nature of that ministry by a similitude, in which the nature of the word and the use of preaching are most appropriately depicted. ... the word of the Lord is seed that is in its own nature fruitful: ministers are as it were husbandmen, that plough and sow. ... but as for making their labor actually productive, that is a miracle of divine grace
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The apostle here compares the establishment of the church at Corinth to the planting of a vine, a tree, or of grain. The figure is taken from agriculture, and the meaning is obvious. Paul established the church. ... The sense here is, that Paul had labored in establishing the church at Corinth; but that subsequently Apollos had labored to increase it, and to build it, up.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: they only plant and water you, but it is the divine blessing on his own husbandry that alone can make it yield fruit. You are not our husbandry, but God's. ... He had employed the former metaphor before, and now he goes on to the other of a building
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: By an image borrowed from the processes of agriculture the Apostle explains the relation in which his teaching stood to that of Apollos — and how all the results were from God. This indication of St. Paul having been the founder, and Apollos the subsequent instructor, of the Corinthian Church
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Paul laid the foundation “as an expert builder”
notes.about: Paul carries a building picture through six verses. He laid the one foundation, Jesus Christ, and others build on it. Gold, silver and precious stones picture work that lasts, which many read as true teaching; wood, hay and straw, work that will not. Fire will prove the quality of each man's work.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: I laid a foundation as an expert builder
figure.means: Paul's work in first preaching Christ at Corinth, the one foundation on which later teachers must build

notes.evidence: John Calvin calls the master builder a most apt similitude: Paul laid the foundation and others must build to match it. Albert Barnes says Paul carries forward the metaphor of the building. T. Teignmouth Shore (Ellicott) sees lasting and passing work set side by side; Simon Browne (Henry's commentary) and Joseph Benson read the materials as true and false teaching.
notes.limit: The writers differ on what the fire is, and on how closely each material stands for a kind of teaching.

cites.quote: As a wise master-builder It is a most apt similitude ... he declares that he had been the first master-builder of God among them in laying the foundation, and that he had with wisdom executed that department of duty, and that it remained that others should go forward in the same manner, regulating the superstructure in conformity with the rule of the foundation.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Paul carries forward the metaphor in this and the following verses with respect to the building. ... Gold is the emblem of that which is valuable and precious, and may be the emblem of that truth and holiness which shall bear the trial of the great Day. ... By this is meant: (1) Errors and false doctrines, such as will not be found to be true on the Day of Judgment
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Some build upon this foundation gold, silver, and precious stones ... namely, those who receive and propagate the pure truths of the gospel ... Others build wood, hay, and stubble, on this foundation; that is, though they adhere to the foundation, they depart from the mind of Christ in many particulars ... The expression carries in it a plain allusion to the refiner's art
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Many ingenious attempts have been made to apply the imagery of this passage in detail to various doctrines or Christian virtues, but it seems best to regard it as broadly and in outline bringing before the reader the two great ideas of permanent and ephemeral work, and the striking contrast between them. The truth brought forward is primarily, if not exclusively, for teachers.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: gold, silver, precious stones The most valuable materials in nature, the most solid, durable, and precious, and which can bear the fire. And here they stand for true, firm, and important doctrines ... wood, hay, and stubble; materials flimsy, unsubstantial, worthless, if compared with the former, and which cannot bear the fire.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Paul calls them “kings” to rebuke their pride
notes.about: Paul tells the Corinthians they already have all they want, are rich, and reign as kings without the apostles. He means the opposite: they only think so, and in their pride they look down on the men through whom they received the gospel. The next verses set the apostles' hardships beside them.

figure.name: Irony
figure.words: Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings.
figure.means: that they only think themselves full, rich and reigning, and are proud of gifts they received

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse as true Irony. Albert Barnes calls it irony and cutting sarcasm, and Calvin says Paul ridicules their self-complacency by irony and upbraids their ingratitude. Simon Browne (Matthew Henry's Commentary) hears a smart irony: they reign only in their own conceit. Adam Clarke judges it a strong irony. On the closing wish, Barnes hears it earnest and Bullinger ironic.
notes.limit: The note is on the first three sentences. Writers differ on the closing wish: some hear the irony go on, while others hear Paul's earnest wish that they truly were as blessed as they thought.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 813
cites.quote: This verse is true Irony. But other figures are involved.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: It is generally agreed that this is spoken in irony, and that it is an indignant sarcasm uttered against the false and self-confident teachers in Corinth. ... The whole passage is an instance of most pungent and cutting sarcasm ... But the more probable interpretation is, that Paul here drops the irony, and addresses them in a sober, earnest manner.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Having in good earnest, and without the use of any figure, beat down their vain confidence, he now also ridicules it by way of irony, because they are so self-complacent, as if they were the happiest persons in the world. ... he tacitly upbraids them with ingratitude, because they had the audacity to despise him, or rather those, through means of whom they had obtained everything.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He presses the duty of humility upon them by a very smart irony, or at least reproves them for their pride and self-conceit ... to intimate how much the Corinthians were elated by the abundance of their wisdom and spiritual gifts ... "You have reigned as kings," says the apostle, "that is, in your own conceit;
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Though this paraphrase appears natural, yet I am of opinion that the apostle here intends a strong irony; and one which, when taken in conjunction with what he had said before, must have stung them to the heart. It is not an unusual thing for many people to forget, if not despise, the men by whom they were brought to the knowledge of the truth
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Love is pictured as a person: patient and kind
notes.about: Paul speaks of love as if it were a person who is patient and kind and does not envy or boast. Giving love the ways of a person makes his account of it lively and moving.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: Love is patient, love is kind
figure.means: love, given the qualities and actions of a person, so that the account of it is lively and moving

notes.evidence: Benson says the apostle here gives love the qualities and actions of a person, to make his account of that divine grace the more lively and affecting.

cites.quote: Here the apostle attributes to love the qualities and actions of a person, in order to render his account of that divine grace the more lively and affecting.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: All they want, then rich, then kings: a climb
notes.about: The three sentences climb: from having all they want, to being rich, to reigning as kings, the highest step of all. Each claim goes beyond the one before it, which shows how highly the Corinthians thought of themselves.

lines.words: Already you have all you want.
Without us, you have become kings.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes calls the third clause a climax: men filled with food, then the rich, then men raised to a throne, the highest elevation. Simon Browne (Henry's Commentary) sees a gradation from sufficiency to wealth and thence to royalty; Calvin says Paul goes step by step, the last much more than the other two; J. A. Bengel calls full, rich, kings a gradation, each step with its own pride.

cites.quote: This is simply carrying forward the idea before stated; but in the form of a climax. The first metaphor is taken from persons “filled with food;” the second from those who are so rich that they do not feel their lack of more; the third from those who are raised to a throne, the highest elevation, where there was nothing further to be reached or desired.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: There is a very elegant gradation from sufficiency to wealth, and thence to royalty, to intimate how much the Corinthians were elated by the abundance of their wisdom and spiritual gifts
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He proceeds, too, step by step, in exposing their insolence. In the first place, he says, that they were full: this refers to the past. He then adds, Ye are rich: this applies to the future. Lastly, he says, that they had reigned as kings this is much more than either of those two.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: A gradation [ascending climax]: full, rich, kings. ... in consequence of fulness, they were fastidious; of opulence, they were insolent; of kingly power, they were proud.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/1_corinthians/4.htm

notes.short: Death is spoken to as a beaten foe
notes.about: Here the chapter breaks into a cry of triumph that speaks to Death as if it were a person, a foe armed with a sting, and asks where its victory and its sting have gone. At the resurrection, death's power to hurt is taken away.

figure.name: Apostrophe
figure.words: Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?
figure.means: Death, spoken to as a person: an enemy whose victory and sting are gone

original.note: In Paul's Greek “sting” is kentron, a point or goad, and the sting of a creature such as a bee or a scorpion.

notes.evidence: Bullinger, under Apostrophe to inanimate things, gives Hosea 13:14 and points to this verse. Clarke says Death is personified here, armed with a sting like a goad. Barnes says the sting is given to death personified, in language of exultation. Simon Browne (Matthew Henry's Commentary) says the saints glory over death as a vanquished enemy.
notes.limit: Some read the cry as Paul's own; others as the song the raised saints will sing over death.

cites.quote: “O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction.” See 1Co 15:55
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Both Death and Hades are here personified: Death is represented as having a sting, dagger, or goad, by which, like the driver of oxen, he is continually irritating and urging on
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The word which is here rendered sting (κέντρον kentron) denotes properly a prick, a point, hence, a goad or stimulus ... It denotes here a venomous thing, or weapon, applied to death personified, as if death employed it to destroy life, as the sting of a bee or a scorpion is used. ... The language here is the language of exultation, as if that was taken away or destroyed.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: They will glory over death as a vanquished enemy, and insult this great and terrible destroyer
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “A little leaven”: a common saying
notes.about: Paul answers the church's boasting with a saying he expects them to know: a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough. One sin left alone in the church, like the man living in sin among them, will spread and spoil the whole. Paul uses the same saying in Galatians 5:9 also.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough
figure.means: one sin, or one sinner, left alone will spread and corrupt the whole church

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, or Proverb, among sayings first in Scripture. Adam Clarke calls it a common maxim and reads the leaven as the sinning man left in the church. Albert Barnes calls it evidently a proverbial saying: one sin allowed in the church spreads through it all. John Calvin says Paul uses a proverbial saying to show a whole multitude infected by one man.
notes.limit: Most of these writers treat it as a saying already in use; one places it among sayings first found in Scripture that later came into general use.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 765
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.” Leaven is always used in a bad sense.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: do you not know and acknowledge the truth of a common maxim, a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? If this leaven - the incestuous person, be permitted to remain among you; if his conduct be not exposed by the most formidable censure; the flood-gates of impurity will be opened on the Church
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This is evidently a proverbial saying. It occurs also in Gal 5:9 . ... A single sin indulged in, or allowed in the church, would act like leaven - it would pervade and corrupt the whole church, unless it was removed.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He makes use of a proverbial saying, by which he intimates that a whole multitude is infected by the contagion of a single individual.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The Passover lamb pointed ahead to Christ
notes.about: Paul calls Christ “our Passover lamb.” The lamb Israel slew at Passover pointed ahead to Him. As Israel put away all leaven when the lamb was slain, so those for whom Christ has been sacrificed are to clear out the old leaven of sin.

figure.name: Type
figure.words: our Passover lamb
figure.means: Christ, whom the lamb slain at Passover pictured ahead of time

original.note: In Paul's Greek the words are to pascha hēmōn, “our Passover”; the word pascha here means the Passover lamb.

notes.evidence: Barnes: no doubt the paschal lamb was a type of the Messiah, designed to typify Him; pascha usually means that lamb. Calvin: Paul explains the correspondence between the figure in the Passover and the reality, Christ sacrificed once. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): as the days of unleavened bread began with the slain lamb, so with Christ slain. Benson: the paschal lamb represented Christ.

cites.quote: There can be no doubt here that the paschal lamb was a type of the Messiah … Our "paschal lamb," for so the word πάσχα pascha usually signifies. … that that lamb was designed to adumbrate or typify him
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Paul, having it in view to exhort the Corinthians to holiness, shows that what was of old figuratively represented in the passover, ought to be at this day accomplished in us, and explains the correspondence which exists between the figure and the reality. … Christ, says Paul, is our Passover He was sacrificed once
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: as the Jews began the days of unleavened bread with the slaying of the Passover lamb, so, Christ our Passover having been already slain, let there be no leaven of evil in you who are the "unleavened lump."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: For even Christ our passover Who was represented by the paschal lamb
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Soldier, vineyard, flock: three pictures from life
notes.about: Paul asks three questions from everyday life. No soldier serves at his own expense, no one plants a vineyard without eating its fruit, no one tends a flock without its milk. Each pictures the minister of the gospel, who may rightly be supported by the church he serves.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not drink of its milk?
figure.means: the minister of the gospel, who like a soldier, a vine planter and a shepherd may rightly live from the work he does

notes.evidence: John Calvin finds three comparisons from common life, showing Paul might live at the church's expense. Albert Barnes counts three illustrations, the ministry compared to warfare and the minister to a soldier. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the minister is spiritually a soldier, a vinedresser and a shepherd; T. Teignmouth Shore (Ellicott), three illustrations from life.
notes.limit: Paul argues for the right here; in verses 12 and 15 he says he did not use it.

cites.quote: Now, by three comparisons, and these, too, taken from common life, he makes it out that it was allowable for him to live, if he chose, at the public expense of the Church, to show that he assumes nothing to himself but what human nature itself teaches us is reasonable. ... As natural equity points out this as reasonable, who will be so unjust as to refuse sustenance to the pastors of the Church?
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: In this verse (7th) the right is enforced by the nature of the case, and by three illustrations. The first is, the right of a soldier or warrior to his wages. The Christian ministry is compared to a warfare, and the Christian minister to a soldier ... The church is often compared to a flock
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The minister is spiritually a soldier ... a vine-dresser ... and a shepherd
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Three illustrations from human life and business show that the principle which has been adopted in the Christian Church is not exceptional. A soldier receives his pay; the planter of a vineyard eats the fruit of it; and the owner of a flock is supported by selling the milk.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: “Voluntary” here means preaching without pay
notes.about: Paul says, “If my preaching is voluntary, I have a reward.” By voluntary he means without pay: the next verse speaks of offering the gospel free of charge. He uses the lesser word to say the greater thing. One writer finds this way of speaking suited to his self-denial.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.words: my preaching is voluntary
figure.means: preaching without pay, offering the gospel free of charge

original.note: In Paul's Greek the word is hekōn, willingly, set beside misthon, a reward: to preach for nothing and yet have a reward.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis (a belittling): Paul means gratuitously, but lessens the wording to increase his meaning. Bengel says willingly stands here for gratuitously, so that with a reward it makes an oxymoron, and that Paul, speaking of his own affairs, often heightens or lessens his words, a way suited to express his self-denial.

cites.quote: “For if I do this thing willingly, I have a reward.” He means gratuitously; but lessens the wording, so as to increase his meaning.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This is here used instead of gratuitously, whence I have a reward makes an oxymoron; ... Paul often, when speaking of his own affairs, uses increase and diminution ... not unlike a catachresis, and suitable to express his self-abnegation.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/1_corinthians/9.htm

notes.short: A race: “Run in such a way as to take the prize”
notes.about: Paul draws a likeness from the races at the games, where all the runners run but only one receives the prize. The Christian is to run in the same way: with all his effort, and on to the end, so as to take the prize.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Run in such a way as to take the prize
figure.means: the Christian life, to be run with a runner's full effort and kept up to the end, so as to win the prize

notes.evidence: John Calvin says Paul borrows a similitude from the race-course: our life is like a race, to be run until death. Albert Barnes says Paul draws on the games near Corinth, one of the most beautiful and bold illustrations. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) finds in them an image of Christian earnestness; Simon Browne (Henry's commentary) says Paul compares himself to the racers.
notes.limit: The likeness lies in the running, not in the one prize: in the games one runner wins, but in the Christian race all who run well may win.

cites.quote: Now he borrows a similitude from the race-course. For as in that case many descend into the arena, but he alone is crowned who has first reached the goal, so there is no reason why any one should feel satisfied with himself on the ground of his having once entered upon the race prescribed in the gospel, unless he persevere in it until death. ... For our life is like a race-course.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: In the remainder of this chapter, Paul illustrates the general sentiment on which he had been dwelling - the duty of practicing self-denial for the salvation of others - by a reference to the well known games which were celebrated near Corinth. ... This is one of the most beautiful, appropriate, vigorous, and bold illustrations that can anywhere be found
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: These periodical games were to the Greeks rather a passion than a mere amusement: hence their suitableness as an image of Christian earnestness. ... The "so" expresses, Run with such perseverance in the heavenly course, as "all" the runners exhibit in the earthly "race" just spoken of: to the end that ye may attain the prize.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Upon this head he compares himself to the racers and combatants in the Isthmian games, an allusion well known to the Corinthians, because they were celebrated in their neighbourhood ... It is quite otherwise in the Christian race than in your races; only one wins the prize in them. You may all run so as to obtain.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Athletes train hard for a crown that fades
notes.about: Paul points to the athletes at the games, who keep strict training for a crown that soon withers. If they deny themselves that much for a perishable crown, believers should deny themselves far more for one that never perishes. Paul then applies it to himself, as runner and as boxer.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline
figure.means: the believer, who should deny himself far more, since he strives for a crown that will never perish

notes.evidence: Calvin calls it a comparison from the athletes, argued from the less to the greater: if they prize a fading crown of leaves, how much more a crown of immortality. Simon Browne (Matthew Henry's commentary) says Paul compares himself to the racers and combatants of the games; T. Teignmouth Shore (Ellicott) sets out the same argument; Barnes says Paul illustrates the duty of self-denial by the games.
notes.limit: The runners of verse 24 begin the same picture; this note takes it up from the athletes' training in verse 25.

cites.quote: This second thing he now sets before them by a comparison taken from pugilists ... Now he argues from the less to the greater, that it is an unseemly thing if we grudge to give up our right ... But if they value so highly a crown of leaves that quickly fades, what value ought we to set upon a crown of immortality?
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Upon this head he compares himself to the racers and combatants in the Isthmian games ... The fighters and wrestlers in your exercises are kept to strict diet and discipline; nay, they keep themselves to it. ... And should not Christians much more abridge themselves of their liberty, for so glorious an end as winning the race, and obtaining the prize set before them?

notes.short: Man and woman, then woman and man, said twice
notes.about: Paul names man, then woman, and turns the pair around: “man did not come from woman, but woman from man.” Verse 9 makes the same turn: “Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.” Repeating the words in reverse order sets the two in contrast.

figure.name: Antimetabole
figure.words: man did not come from woman, but woman from man
figure.means: the man and the woman contrasted: the woman came from the man, not the man from the woman

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists verses 8 and 9 under Antimetabole, or Counterchange, which he defines as words repeated in reverse order to oppose one thing to another or to contrast two or more things. He sets out both turns: man and woman, then woman and man, in verse 8, and the same again in verse 9.
notes.limit: The note is about how the words are set out, not the whole teaching: verses 11 and 12 add that in the Lord “woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman.”

notes.short: The church is like one body with many parts
notes.about: Paul pictures the human body: one body of many parts, each one needed, none able to say to another “I do not need you.” So it is with Christ's people. notes.short: Our knowledge now is a child's beside heaven's
notes.about: Paul recalls how as a child he talked, thought and reasoned like a child, and set those ways aside when he became a man. The likeness shows that what we know in this life is like a child's knowledge beside what we will know in the life to come, when the partial passes away.

notes.short: Flute, harp and trumpet: sounds must be clear
notes.about: Paul points to the flute and harp, whose tune no one can tell unless the notes are distinct, and to a trumpet whose muffled call leaves soldiers unready for battle. Speech in the church that the hearers cannot understand is just as useless to them.

figure.words: Even in the case of lifeless instruments, such as the flute or harp
figure.means: speaking in tongues no one understands: like notes with no clear tune, it tells the hearers nothing and builds no one up

notes.short: Paul calls himself least, and God's grace stands out
notes.about: Paul calls himself the least of the apostles, unworthy of the name, because he persecuted the church. figure.means: Paul lowers himself, so that the grace of God that made him an apostle is seen the greater

Simon Browne (Matthew Henry's Commentary) says Paul, the more he worked, grew humbler and readier to magnify God's favour.
notes.limit: One writer thinks Paul was also answering those at Corinth who belittled him; another adds that he was least because he was the last of the apostles to be called.

notes.short: A seed must die before it comes to life

notes.short: Sun, moon and stars picture the raised body
notes.about: Paul points to what God has made. Heavenly bodies differ from earthly ones, and sun, moon and stars each have their own splendor. figure.name: Simile
